q: A 2.0 m long steel bar of 20 mm diameter carries an axial tension of 50 kN. Taking $E = 200\ \mathrm{GPa}$, the elongation is closest to:
explain: $A = \pi \cdot 20^2/4 = 314.2\ \mathrm{mm^2}$; $\sigma = 50\,000/314.2 = 159.2\ \mathrm{N/mm^2}$; $\delta = \sigma L/E = 159.2 \times 2000 / 200\,000 = 1.59\ \mathrm{mm}$. 6.37 mm results from mixing up radius and diameter ($A = \pi r^2/4 = 78.5\ \mathrm{mm^2}$).

q: For a concrete mix with fixed cement content and aggregate grading, increasing the free water/cement ratio will most likely:
options: Increase workability and reduce strength and durability
Have no effect on strength provided curing is adequate
Increase both workability and long-term durability
explain: More free water increases slump/workability but raises capillary porosity in the hardened paste (Abrams' law), lowering strength and increasing permeability, hence reducing durability.

q: A prestressing strand is stretched and its ends are held at a fixed length. Over time the force in the strand reduces. This phenomenon is:
explain: Relaxation is loss of stress under constant strain. Creep is increase of strain under constant stress; creep rupture is failure under sustained stress; fatigue is damage under cyclic stress.

q: A higher carbon equivalent value (CEV) of a structural steel primarily indicates:
options: Better weldability and lower preheat requirement
Greater susceptibility to hydrogen cracking in the heat-affected zone
explain: CEV combines C, Mn, Cr, Mo, V, Ni, Cu content as a measure of hardenability. Higher CEV → harder, more brittle HAZ martensite → greater risk of hydrogen-induced cold cracking; more preheat is needed (EN 1011-2).

A beam fixed at both ends, span 5 m, carries a UDL of 12 kN/m. The fixed-end moment at each support is:
explain: $\mathrm{FEM} = wL^2/12 = 12 \times 5^2 / 12 = 25\ \mathrm{kNm}$ (37.5 kNm is the propped-cantilever value $wL^2/8$).

q: At joint B, member BA (length 4 m, far end A fixed) and member BC (length 6 m, far end C pinned) meet. Both have the same EI. The distribution factor for BA is:
A fixed-ended beam of span 6 m with uniform plastic moment $M_p = 120\ \mathrm{kNm}$ carries a central point load. The plastic collapse load is:
explain: Three hinges (two supports + midspan). Virtual work: $P \cdot (L/2)\theta = M_p(\theta + 2\theta + \theta)$ → $P = 8M_p/L = 8 \times 120/6 = 160\ \mathrm{kN}$.

q: A vertical column 5 m tall is fixed at its base and completely free at the top. $E = 210\ \mathrm{GPa}$ and $I = 25 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$. The elastic critical (Euler) load is closest to:
explain: Fixed–free: $L_{\mathrm{cr}} = 2L = 10\ \mathrm{m}$. $N_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2EI/L_{\mathrm{cr}}^2 = \pi^2 \times 210\,000 \times 25 \times 10^6 / 10\,000^2 = 518\ \mathrm{kN}$. 2073 kN results from wrongly using $L_{\mathrm{cr}} = L$.

q: A soil has $G_s = 2.70$, void ratio $e = 0.65$ and water content $w = 18\,\%$. Taking $\gamma_w = 9.81\ \mathrm{kN/m^3}$, its bulk unit weight is closest to:

A uniform deposit has $\gamma = 18\ \mathrm{kN/m^3}$ above the water table and $\gamma_{\mathrm{sat}} = 20\ \mathrm{kN/m^3}$ below it. The water table is 2 m below ground. The vertical effective stress at 6 m depth is closest to ($\gamma_w = 9.81\ \mathrm{kN/m^3}$):
A 6 m thick clay layer is drained at both top and bottom, with $c_v = 2\ \mathrm{m^2}$/year. The time for 50% average consolidation ($T_v = 0.197$) is closest to:
explain: Double drainage → $H_{\mathrm{dr}} = 3\ \mathrm{m}$. $t = T_v H_{\mathrm{dr}}^2/c_v = 0.197 \times 9/2 = 0.89\ \mathrm{years}$. 3.55 years results from single drainage ($H_{\mathrm{dr}} = 6\ \mathrm{m}$).

q: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge at the free water surface. The resultant hydrostatic thrust on the gate is closest to ($\rho = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$):
explain: $F = \rho g h_c A = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 1.5 \times (2 \times 3) = 88.3\ \mathrm{kN}$, acting at the centre of pressure 2.0 m below the surface (2/3 of the height).

q: Water ($\rho = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$) flows at $0.10\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$ through a horizontal pipe that contracts from 300 mm to 150 mm diameter. Neglecting losses, the pressure drop across the contraction is closest to:
A 1:25 undistorted Froude-scaled model of a spillway passes $0.02\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$. The corresponding prototype discharge is:
According to Griffith theory, if the critical flaw length in a brittle material is increased fourfold, its fracture strength becomes:
explain: $\sigma_f = \sqrt{2E\gamma_s/\pi c} \propto 1/\sqrt{c}$. Four times the crack length → $1/\sqrt{4} = \tfrac12$ of the original strength.

q: A steel bar ($\nu = 0.30$) is stretched to an axial strain of 0.001. The approximate unit volume change is:
explain: $\Delta V/V \approx \varepsilon(1 - 2\nu) = 0.001 \times (1 - 0.6) = +4 \times 10^{-4}$. Volume increases in tension for $\nu < 0.5$ (the cross-sectional area shrinks, but less than the length grows).

q: A component cycles between a maximum stress of +150 MPa and a minimum of −50 MPa. The stress amplitude is:
explain: $\sigma_a = (\sigma_{\mathrm{max}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{min}})/2 = (150 - (-50))/2 = 100\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Mean stress = 50 MPa; stress range = 200 MPa; $R = \sigma_{\mathrm{min}}/\sigma_{\mathrm{max}} = -0.33$.

q: A steel has C 0.18 %, Mn 1.20 %, Cr 0.10 %, Mo 0.05 %, V 0.02 %, Cu 0.15 %, Ni 0.10 %. Its carbon equivalent $\mathrm{CE} = \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{Mn}/6 + (\mathrm{Cr} + \mathrm{Mo} + \mathrm{V})/5 + (\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{Ni})/15$ is closest to:
A 1.20 m length of deformed reinforcing bar weighs 4.62 kg. Using $A = M/(0.00785 L)$, its nominal diameter is:
Even at complete hydration, capillary pores remain in cement paste when the water/cement ratio exceeds about:
explain: Chemically combined water ≈ 0.20–0.24; with gel water, $w/c \approx 0.36\text{–}0.38$ is needed to fill the space. Above that, capillary pores persist.

q: A mix has $450\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ OPC, $35\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ silica fume (efficiency factor $k = 3$) and $160\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ free water. The effective water/cement ratio for strength is closest to:
explain: $(w/c)_{\mathrm{eff}} = W/(C + kS) = 160/(450 + 3 \times 35) = 160/555 = 0.29$. (The plain water/binder ratio is $160/485 = 0.33$.)

q: Per $\mathrm{m^3}$: cement 350 kg (density 3150), water 175 kg, sand 750 kg (density 2600), air 2 %. The mass of coarse aggregate (density $2650\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$) is closest to:
With 9 rebound-hammer readings at a location, the mean rebound number is expected (95 % confidence) to be within about:
A 100 × 100 mm prism on a 300 mm span fails at 12 kN in four-point bending. Using $f = Fl/(d_1d_2^2)$, the flexural strength is:
A cement contains $0.25\,\% \mathrm{Na_2O}$ and $0.60\,\% \mathrm{K_2O}$. Its equivalent alkali content and classification are:
explain: $\mathrm{Na_2O_{eq}} = 0.25 + 0.658 \times 0.60 = 0.645\,\% > 0.60\,\%$ → not a low-alkali cement, so take extra ASR precautions with reactive aggregate.

q: Three coplanar concurrent forces act on a particle: 20 kN at 0°, 30 kN at 60° and 25 kN at 150° (angles from the +x axis). The magnitude of the resultant is closest to:

A vertical bar is fixed at top A and bottom B. Segment AC is 300 mm long with $A = 300\ \mathrm{mm^2}$; segment CB is 300 mm long with $A = 500\ \mathrm{mm^2}$; same E. A 400 kN downward load acts at C. The reaction at B is:
explain: Compatibility ($\delta_{\mathrm{AC}} = \delta_{\mathrm{CB}}$): $R_A \cdot L/A_1 = R_B \cdot L/A_2$ with $R_A + R_B = 400$. Flexibilities 1/300 : 1/500 → $R_B = 400 \times (1/300)/(1/300 + 1/500) = 250\ \mathrm{kN}$ (compression in CB); $R_A = 150\ \mathrm{kN}$.

q: A hollow circular shaft (outer Ø 100 mm, inner Ø 60 mm) transmits a torque of 10 kNm. The maximum shear stress is closest to:
explain: $J = \pi(100^4 - 60^4)/32 = 8.55 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$; $\tau_{\mathrm{max}} = Tc/J = 10 \times 10^6 \times 50/8.55 \times 10^6 = 58.5\ \mathrm{MPa}$. (50.9 MPa is a solid 100 mm shaft.)

q: A 50 mm solid steel shaft, 2 m long ($G = 80\ \mathrm{GPa}$), carries a torque of 1 kNm. The angle of twist is closest to:

A simply supported beam (span 6 m, $EI = 20\,000\ \mathrm{kNm^2}$) carries a central point load of 40 kN. Using moment-area, the end slope is:
explain: By symmetry the slope at midspan is zero; $\theta_A$ = area of M/EI from A to midspan = $\tfrac12 \times (L/2) \times (PL/4)/EI = PL^2/(16EI) = 40 \times 36/(16 \times 20\,000) = 0.0045\ \mathrm{rad}$.

q: A symmetric gable frame has 4 members and 5 joints, pinned at both bases ($r = 4$) with an internal hinge at the apex ($c = 1$). Using 3m + r vs 3j + c, the frame is:
explain: $3m + r = 12 + 4 = 16$; $3j + c = 15 + 1 = 16$ → equal → statically determinate (a three-pinned frame), given no geometric instability.

A truss member with $EA/L = 50\ \mathrm{MN/m}$ is inclined at 30° to the global x-axis. The global stiffness term $k_{11} = (EA/L)\lambda_x^2$ is:
A mercury U-tube manometer (SG 13.6) connected across two points in a water pipe at the same elevation shows a 200 mm deflection. The pressure difference is closest to:
explain: $\Delta p = (\rho_{\mathrm{Hg}} - \rho_w)g \cdot h = (13.6 - 1) \times 9810 \times 0.2 = 24.7\ \mathrm{kPa}$. (26.7 kPa ignores the water column above the mercury.)

q: A vertical rectangular gate, 2 m wide and 3 m high, has its top edge 1 m below the water surface. The depth of the centre of pressure is:
A quarter-circle gate of radius 2 m and width 3 m retains water on its concave side, with water level at the top of the gate. The vertical force component is closest to:
explain: $F_V$ = weight of water above = $\rho g(\pi R^2/4)w = 9.81 \times \pi \times 3 = 92.5\ \mathrm{kN}$. $F_H = \rho g(R/2)(R \cdot w) = 58.9\ \mathrm{kN}$; resultant 109.6 kN.

q: A timber block 2 m × 0.5 m × 0.5 m (density $650\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$) floats in seawater ($1025\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$) with its long axis horizontal. Its draft is closest to:
A rectangular pontoon 20 m long and 6 m wide floats at a draft of 1.5 m with its centre of gravity 2.0 m above the keel. The metacentric height for rolling is:
explain: $\mathrm{BM} = I/V = (L \cdot B^3/12)/(L \cdot B \cdot d) = B^2/(12d) = 36/18 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$; $\mathrm{KB} = d/2 = 0.75\ \mathrm{m}$; $\mathrm{GM} = \mathrm{KB} + \mathrm{BM} - \mathrm{KG} = 0.75 + 2.0 - 2.0 = 0.75\ \mathrm{m}$ (> 0, stable).

Water flows at $0.2\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$ round a horizontal 90° bend in a 300 mm pipe. Neglecting pressure and weight, the magnitude of the resultant force on the bend is closest to:
explain: $v = 0.2/(\pi \times 0.3^2/4) = 2.83\ \mathrm{m/s}$; $\rho Qv = 1000 \times 0.2 \times 2.83 = 566\ \mathrm{N}$ in each of x and y → resultant $\sqrt{2} \times 566 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$.

q: A 16 mm pin in double shear connects a member carrying 20 kN. The average shear stress in the pin is closest to:
explain: Double shear: $V = P/2 = 10\ \mathrm{kN}$ on each plane; $\tau = V/A = 10\,000/(\pi \times 16^2/4) = 49.7\ \mathrm{MPa}$. (99.5 MPa would be single shear.)

q: A shaft transmits 50 kW at 300 rpm. The torque in the shaft is closest to:
A timber beam ($E = 10\ \mathrm{GPa}$) is reinforced with a 100 mm wide steel plate ($E = 200\ \mathrm{GPa}$). In the transformed section expressed in timber, the plate's equivalent width is:
explain: $n = E_{\mathrm{steel}}/E_{\mathrm{timber}} = 20$; scale widths only: $b^* = 20 \times 100 = 2000\ \mathrm{mm}$ (depth unchanged). Steel stress = $n \times (My/I)$ of the transformed section.

q: A 4 m cantilever ($EI = 20\,000\ \mathrm{kNm^2}$) carries a UDL of 10 kN/m. Using moment-area (parabolic spandrel: area bh/3, centroid 3b/4 from the vertex), the tip deflection is:
explain: M/EI spandrel: $h = wL^2/(2EI)$, area $= Lh/3 = wL^3/(6EI)$, centroid 3L/4 from the tip → $\delta = wL^4/(8EI) = 10 \times 256/(8 \times 20\,000) = 0.016\ \mathrm{m} = 16\ \mathrm{mm}$.

q: Two forces of 80 N and 120 N act at a point with 60° between their lines of action. Using the cosine rule, the resultant is closest to:
explain: Parallelogram: $R^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab \cos\theta = 6400 + 14\,400 + 2 \times 80 \times 120 \times 0.5 = 30\,400$ → $R = 174.4\ \mathrm{N}$. (105.8 N wrongly uses $-2ab \cos\theta$ with the included angle of the force triangle mistaken.)

q: A cable spans 10 m between supports at the same level and carries a single 20 kN load at midspan with a sag of 1.0 m (cable weight neglected). The maximum cable tension is closest to:
explain: Vertical reactions 10 kN each. Moment about the load point for half the cable: $H \times 1.0 = 10 \times 5$ → $H = 50\ \mathrm{kN}$. $T_{\mathrm{max}} = \sqrt{50^2 + 10^2} = 51.0\ \mathrm{kN}$ (at the supports).
